name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: The single best cross-department improvement is to standardize a shared "decision log" template across all teams. This ensures every major choice—from creative direction to technical constraints—is documented in one place with clear ownership, reasons, and trade-offs. The trade-off is slower initial setup for faster alignment later. Engineering owns the template; all departments contribute entries.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s “shared decision log” risks becoming a graveyard of stale checkboxes—teams will dump half-baked reasons just to clear the template, not to inform future decisions. Instead, enforce a *living* artifact: a single, searchable “decision ledger” where every entry must cite a concrete future action or deadline; anything older than 90 days auto-expires unless renewed by the original decider. That settles it: the lead publishes the ledger with the purge rule and the first 10 entries within two weeks.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt Scriv’s “living decision ledger” with mandatory future-action citations. Every major choice—creative, technical, or operational—must include the next concrete step it triggers, ensuring entries stay useful instead of decorative. The trade-off is stricter upfront effort: teams must articulate follow-up actions, not just log decisions. This single artifact becomes the single source of truth for why we did what we did and what happens next.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s “living ledger” solves the graveyard problem but risks turning every decision into a bureaucratic audit—teams will game the system by padding entries with trivial next steps just to comply. Instead, enforce a *lightweight* artifact: a shared Notion board where every major choice gets a one-line summary, a link to the full rationale, and a single owner who updates it only when the decision’s impact changes. That settles it: low overhead, high signal, no checkbox theater.

name: Scope
text: Adopt Scriv’s “living decision ledger” with mandatory future-action citations. Every major choice—creative, technical, or operational—must include the next concrete step it triggers, ensuring entries stay useful instead of decorative. The trade-off is stricter upfront effort: teams must articulate follow-up actions, not just log decisions. This beats a graveyard of stale entries or a bureaucratic audit by forcing real accountability.

name: Scriv
text: The "living decision ledger" still risks becoming a compliance chore—teams will pad entries with trivial next steps just to check the box. Instead, enforce a *minimal* artifact: a shared Slack channel where every major decision gets a single, timestamped message with a future-action citation. The lead is the person who owns the decision’s outcome, and the artifact exists when the message is posted.

name: Reel
text: Adopt Scriv’s “living decision ledger” with mandatory future-action citations. Every major choice—creative, technical, or operational—must include the next concrete step it triggers, ensuring entries stay useful instead of decorative. The trade-off is stricter upfront effort: teams must articulate follow-ups immediately, not just log decisions. This beats a Notion board or Slack channel because it forces real ownership, not just visibility.

name: Scriv
text: Slack’s ephemeral format guarantees decisions vanish into the scroll—no one will search a year-old thread for the *why* behind a choice. Instead, adopt a lightweight living ledger in Notion where each entry is a one-sentence decision + one-sentence future action, no more; settle the argument by measuring how often teams reference past entries in their next major choice.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt a *minimal* Notion board where every major decision gets a single entry: one sentence for the choice, one sentence for the next concrete step, timestamped. This keeps the ledger lightweight enough to actually use while forcing clarity on consequences—no padding possible. The trade-off is losing the richer detail of Scriv’s ledger, but that depth rarely survives the next cycle anyway.

name: Sift
text: The Notion ledger risks becoming a graveyard of stale entries—teams will dump decisions there and never revisit them. Instead, enforce a *living* Slack channel where each decision is a pinned message with a future-action citation; the timestamped thread forces visibility and the pinned message guarantees it’s never buried. Settle the argument by measuring how often teams reference past decisions in their work.

name: Scope
text: Adopt Chisel’s minimal Notion board: one sentence per decision, one sentence for the next concrete step, timestamped. It balances clarity with durability—unlike Slack, Notion won’t bury decisions, and unlike padded ledgers, the brevity prevents decay. Trade-off: teams must resist over-engineering the board, but the constraint itself enforces discipline. Done when the board exists with 10 entries.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Notion’s search is still too slow—teams will treat the ledger as a dumping ground, not a tool. Instead, enforce a *public* Google Doc with a simple table: Decision | Next Action | Owner | Due Date. The flat structure forces ownership and deadlines, and the doc’s version history settles disputes. The risk? Overhead if we let it bloat—settle it by capping each entry to 30 seconds of work to add.

name: Reel
text: Adopt Scriv’s *living decision ledger* in a public Google Doc with a table: Decision | Next Action | Owner | Due Date. The flat structure forces ownership and deadlines, and the doc’s version history settles disputes without slowing teams down. Trade-off: teams must resist over-engineering the table—keep it minimal or it becomes a chore.
